tldr: A post-training quantization framework that quantizes both weights and activations of VLA models to 4-bit (W4A4) without policy retraining, achieving fast and accurate physical robot execution on edge devices like the Jetson AGX Orin.
hero_caption: Overview of FoldQuantVLA. (a) shows the scope: keeping vision and decoders in floating point while quantizing linear layers in the language backbone and action expert to low bits. (b) illustrates the mechanism: fixing a single transform for shared activations and folding its inverse into subsequent weight matrices, achieving both runtime consistency and speedups.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine vision, language, and action generation, but both the language backbone and iterative denoising action expert lie directly on the latency-critical path. This poses a major bottleneck for smooth real-time robot control. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) has gained attention as a way to compress models. However, standard channel scaling and rotation transforms used to suppress activation outliers can cause basis mismatches across multiple consumer branches or introduce unwanted runtime overhead.

To solve this, the authors introduce "FoldQuantVLA," a framework that assigns exactly one common basis transform per shared activation site and folds its inverse entirely into downstream weight matrices offline. Combined with fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms and dynamic per-token quantization at runtime, it eliminates diffusion-step scale lookup tables and enables native low-bit integer matrix multiplication in the transformed coordinates using offline optimal rounding (GPTQ).

Evaluation spans simulation environments (LIBERO, SimplerEnv) as well as tabletop arms (ALOHA, SO-101) using state-of-the-art models like GR00T and $\pi_{0.5}$. On Jetson AGX Orin, it achieves a $1.20$ to $1.33\times$ speedup over floating-point TensorRT engines. Furthermore, by adopting "Selective INT8"—retaining only error-sensitive language layers (o_proj and down_proj) at 8 bits (W8A8)—real-robot task success climbs from $80.0\%$ to $92.5\%$, while adding only 1 ms of latency on Orin.
contributions: Formulated the "Consistent Folding" convention, which assigns a single transform basis to shared activations across multiple branches and folds the inverse transform into weights, preserving consistency from calibration to native execution.
Established a W4A4 recipe for VLAs combining channel scaling, fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms (FWHT), and per-token dynamic quantization, removing the need for per-diffusion-step scale tables.

Demonstrated that selectively retaining the language backbone attention-output (o_proj) and feed-forward down-projection (down_proj) at 8 bits (W8A8) dramatically improves real-robot success with minimal latency overhead.
Developed CUTLASS-based custom TensorRT plugins for Ada GPUs and Jetson AGX Orin, demonstrating that native W4A4 inference speeds surpass optimized floating-point engines on real hardware.

sections.heading: Why is VLA quantization hard, and what does it take?
sections.summary: Because language backbones and iterative action experts account for most VLA latency, cutting latency without degrading closed-loop control is essential. This paper introduces FoldQuantVLA, quantizing weights and activations to 4 bits (W4A4) without retraining while preserving real-robot performance through consistent coordinate transforms and selective INT8.
sections.details:
VLA models for robotics combine image processing, language models, and an action expert that iteratively denoises to generate chunks of actions. In robot control, a slight deviation in generated actions alters subsequent observations, making precision preservation far more demanding than in standard language models.

In post-training quantization (PTQ) without retraining, channel scaling and rotation transforms are widely adopted to suppress extreme outliers. However, applying these naively to activations shared by multiple operations creates coordinate mismatches between calibration and runtime. This paper addresses this by assigning a single basis transform to each shared activation site and folding its inverse offline into the weight matrices of subsequent linear projections.

Additionally, the authors introduce a "Selective INT8" configuration that keeps only the most sensitive output projections in the language model at 8 bits. With just a 1 ms latency increase on Jetson AGX Orin, this dramatically boosts real-robot success rates from 80.0% to 92.5%.

sections.heading: Prior work on activation transforms and VLA quantization
sections.summary: This section reviews equivalence transforms and quantization techniques for LLMs and diffusion models (SmoothQuant, QuaRot, SVDQuant, etc.), alongside recent VLA quantization studies. FoldQuantVLA focuses on rigorous coordinate consistency across multiple consumer ops and native low-bit execution at batch size 1.
sections.details:
In LLM quantization, several methods have been proposed to mitigate activation outliers, including per-channel scaling with SmoothQuant, outlier dispersion via orthogonal rotations with QuaRot, and learned rotation matrices with SpinQuant. Furthermore, GPTQ for second-order weight rounding and AWQ for protecting salient channels are widely used.

To bridge these methods with deployment hardware, serving frameworks like Atom and QServe, as well as SVDQuant for 4-bit diffusion models, have emerged. In the VLA domain, works such as QuantVLA and HoloQ-VLA have explored temporal precision allocation and SVD-Hadamard rotations.

FoldQuantVLA distinguishes itself by preserving strict coordinate consistency across the entire execution graph with shared nodes, enabling native low-bit integer GEMM in both the language backbone and action expert for batch size 1 real-robot deployments.

sections.heading: How FoldQuantVLA works: consistent folding and execution architecture
sections.summary: A single invertible transform is applied to shared activations, and its inverse is pre-folded into all downstream weights to suppress outliers without adding runtime overhead. It further incorporates fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms, per-token dynamic quantization, GPTQ rounding, and selective INT8 for sensitive layers.
sections.details:
### III-A Scope and Execution Model
A VLA model maps observation images, language instructions, and initial noise to actions. This work targets the linear projection layers (GEMMs) in the computationally heavy language backbone $\mathcal{L}$ and action expert $\mathcal{E}$. The visual encoder, attention softmax operations, LayerNorm, residual additions, and action decoder remain in floating point. Activations use dynamic per-token scaling, while weights use per-output-channel scaling. A preliminary study showed that in the most extreme outlier layer, activation spread (maximum / median) reaches ~550,000 across the entire tensor, whereas token-wise scaling bounds it to ~8,600, demonstrating that per-token scaling is essential.

### III-B Consistent Folding
For a linear projection $y = Wx + b$, introducing an invertible transform $T$ such that $z = Tx$ and $\widetilde{W} = W T^{-1}$ guarantees strict equivalence before quantization: $\widetilde{W}z + b = Wx + b$. However, when an activation $x_v$ branches into multiple projections (such as Query, Key, and Value projections), all consumers must share the exact same $T_v$, with $T_v^{-1}$ pre-folded into each weight matrix. Using different transforms across consumers creates coordinate mismatch errors, drastically lowering output action fidelity (cosine similarity).

### III-C & D Supported Transforms and Normalization Layers
Transforms combine orthogonal rotations $R_v$ and diagonal scaling matrices. In the language model, normalized block Hadamard transforms with block size $\beta=64$ are adopted. These are implemented as fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms (FWHT) with an $O(d_v \log \beta)$ complexity. For projections immediately following RMSNorm, the diagonal scale is absorbed directly into the learned gain parameter of RMSNorm instead of being inserted as an explicit division before GEMM, eliminating runtime division overhead.

### III-E & F Offline Parameters and Native Execution
By using dynamic per-token scaling, all diffusion steps can be handled by the same engine without maintaining per-step scale lookup tables. In the transformed coordinates, weights are rounded to INT4 using GPTQ to minimize reconstruction error. The inference runtime uses custom TensorRT plugins built with CUTLASS v3.6.0, executing signed INT4 weight and activation matrix multiplies with native INT32 accumulators.

### III-G Selective INT8
Building upon uniform W4A4, this configuration retains two particularly error-sensitive layers at W8A8: the attention output projection (o_proj) and feed-forward down-projection (down_proj) in the language backbone. These layers feed directly into the residual stream and exhibit the largest outlier spreads. Raising only these two layers to 8 bits without retraining dramatically restores output action fidelity.

captions.F3: Flowchart of the FoldQuantVLA execution pipeline and folding mechanism. At build time, common transforms $T_v$ are determined offline and their inverses folded into downstream weights $\widetilde{W}_i$. At runtime, transformation and quantization happen once before feeding into each GEMM without redundant computation.

sections.heading: Evaluation setup and experimental protocol
sections.summary: The method is comprehensively evaluated across three generations of GR00T (N1.5, N1.6, N1.7) and $\pi_{0.5}$ on simulators (LIBERO, SimplerEnv) and physical robots (ALOHA, SO-101). Latency is benchmarked on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER and Jetson AGX Orin.
sections.details:
Evaluation covers open-source VLA checkpoints: the GR00T family (N1.7, N1.6, N1.5) and $\pi_{0.5}$. GR00T denoises in 4 steps to predict 16 action chunks, executing the first 1 to 8 steps. $\pi_{0.5}$ denoises in 10 steps and executes 5 out of 10 steps.

The experimental protocol includes:
- **Numerical Fidelity**: Measures cosine similarity (directional agreement) and maximum coordinate error (magnitude deviation) of decoded action vectors against the floating-point (BF16) model under identical noise.
- **Simulation Verification (LIBERO)**: Evaluates success rates across four suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, 100), totaling 40 tasks with 20 initial states each (800 episodes total).
- **SimplerEnv Bridge**: Evaluates GR00T N1.6 control performance across 7 tasks using a simulated WidowX robot arm.
- **Latency Benchmarking**: Measures wall-clock time from observation input to action output at batch size 1 on a desktop GPU (RTX 4070 Ti SUPER) and an embedded platform (Jetson AGX Orin).

sections.heading: Simulation comparison with prior W4A4 recipes
sections.summary: On the LIBERO benchmark, FoldQuantVLA was compared against ported baselines of prior low-bit methods (HoloQ-VLA and DuQuant). FoldQuantVLA matches or exceeds the success rates of these earlier methods.
sections.details:
Comparing average task success on LIBERO, FoldQuantVLA (FQ W4A4) achieved 94.6% on GR00T N1.7, and the selective INT8 variant (FQ W4A4 + o/d INT8) reached 95.0%, outperforming the HoloQ-VLA port (92.9%) and the DuQuant port (93.4%).

For the $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint, the selective INT8 variant scored 97.8%, coming very close to the 98.0% reported in the original HoloQ-VLA paper. While prior techniques required complicated procedures like maintaining distinct scale parameters per diffusion step, FoldQuantVLA achieves competitive accuracy using simple dynamic quantization combined with consistent basis transforms.

sections.heading: Latency gains and memory savings from native low-bit deployment
sections.summary: On Jetson AGX Orin, FoldQuantVLA delivers $1.20$ to $1.33\times$ speedups over optimized floating-point TensorRT engines. Weight memory is cut to roughly a quarter, and the selective INT8 overhead is just 1 to 3 ms on Orin.
sections.details:
### VI-A Acceleration Beyond Floating-Point Engines
Simply compiling PyTorch eager models yields an 83–92% latency reduction. FoldQuantVLA achieves an additional $1.20$ to $1.33\times$ speedup on Orin and $1.25$ to $1.52\times$ on a desktop GPU over compiled floating-point TensorRT engines. Notably, existing ModelOpt W4A16 AWQ (weight-only INT4) runs slower than floating point at batch size 1, proving that native W4A4 arithmetic—quantizing activations alongside weights—is essential.

### VI-B Added Cost of Selective INT8
Reverting o_proj and down_proj back to INT8 adds negligible delay: 0.4 to 1.8 ms on the desktop GPU and only 1 to 3 ms on Orin for GR00T models. For example, running N1.7 on Orin takes 119 ms under uniform W4A4 and 120 ms under selective INT8. This remains substantially faster than W8A8 (127 ms) and floating-point (146 ms).

### VI-C Storage and Memory Footprint
For GR00T N1.6, weight parameter storage drops by ~73%, from 3802 MB in floating-point down to 1011 MB in W4A4. The selective INT8 configuration remains almost as compact at 1189 MB.

sections.heading: Accuracy evaluation and the dramatic impact of selective INT8
sections.summary: Simulations on LIBERO and SimplerEnv, paired with action vector fidelity analysis, show that while overall simulator averages can hide degradation, selective INT8 effectively rescues worst-case cosine similarity drops and task collapses.
sections.details:
### VII-A & B Deep-Dive into Simulation Results
In the 800-episode LIBERO benchmark, differences in success rate between W4A4 and selective INT8 were hard to detect statistically. However, detailed SimplerEnv results on the WidowX arm revealed that uniform W4A4 caused a 34.5 percentage point collapse on the "put item in basket" task compared to BF16. Adding selective INT8 restored success on that task from 58.0% to 70.5% and boosted drawer opening from 81.5% to 92.0%, preventing individual task failures.

### VII-C & D Held-Out Fidelity and Ablations
Evaluating cosine similarity on held-out trajectories not used in calibration showed that uniform W4A4 suffered worst-case drops down to 0.461 (N1.6) and 0.802 (N1.7). A few severe failure inferences pulled down overall accuracy. Selective INT8 raised these minimum similarities to 0.850 and 0.912, respectively, and cut the median maximum coordinate error nearly in half.

Ablation experiments confirmed that transform basis mismatches severely degrade offline accuracy, and that GPTQ weight rounding provides superior fidelity compared to simple round-to-nearest (RTN).

sections.heading: Real-robot trials: a 1 ms latency addition lifts success to 92.5%
sections.summary: Testing across four tasks on robot arms (ALOHA, SO-101) powered by Jetson AGX Orin showed that selective INT8 increased N1.7 success from 80.0% with uniform W4A4 to 92.5%, surpassing the baseline floating-point model (90.0%).
sections.details:
Real-robot trials used a single-arm ALOHA and a low-cost SO-101 arm across four tasks: putting a banana in a pot and covering it with a lid, and placing or stacking blocks in cups (80 trials per configuration).

The results were striking. While uniform W4A4 achieved an 80.0% success rate, "FQ W4A4 + o/d INT8" (keeping just two language layers at 8-bit) outperformed uniform W4A4 across all tasks, reaching a pooled success rate of 92.5%. This equals or exceeds floating-point TensorRT (90.0%) and BF16 PyTorch (87.5%). The latency increase on Orin was only 1 ms (119 ms to 120 ms), proving to be an exceptionally cost-effective boost.

In contrast, standard ModelOpt W8A8 SmoothQuant using static per-tensor scales caused violent jitter that threatened robot hardware, forcing trials to abort early. This underscores the necessity of sound low-bit quantization design for VLAs.

captions.F5: Successful executions across four real-robot tasks (T1 to T4). T1 (ALOHA) and T2 (SO-101) involve placing a banana in a pot and covering it with a lid; T3 involves sweeping all blocks into a cup; T4 requires precisely stacking a blue block onto a red block.

sections.heading: Limitations and reproducibility caveats
sections.summary: The authors honestly report architectural sensitivities—where SmolVLA and Evo-1 suffered notable drops—as well as hardware nuances, such as native INT4 falling back to INT8 on H100 GPUs.
sections.details:
The authors frankly discuss the limitations of their approach:

- **Architecture Sensitivity**: While FoldQuantVLA worked exceptionally well on GR00T and $\pi_{0.5}$, preliminary experiments on other VLA architectures such as SmolVLA (dropping from 71.1% in BF16 to 27.1% in W4A4) and Evo-1 (dropping from 91.6% to 81.0%) showed severe performance degradation. It is not unconditionally universal across all VLAs.
- **Native Hardware Execution**: True INT4$\times$INT4 hardware acceleration is validated on Ada GPUs and Jetson AGX Orin. On the NVIDIA H100 used in experiments, execution fell back to INT8 downcasting in the backend. Thus, H100 results do not reflect native INT4 speeds or bit-level equivalence.
- **Evaluation Scale**: Real-robot experiments used 20 trials per task, requiring larger sample sizes to establish conclusive statistical significance. The authors also highlight metric limitations: high action vector cosine similarity does not always guarantee high closed-loop task success.

sections.heading: Conclusion: a major step toward practical edge VLAs
sections.summary: FoldQuantVLA makes W4A4 VLA inference viable by maintaining transform consistency from calibration through native execution. In particular, selective INT8—adding just 1 ms of latency to achieve 92.5% real-robot success—offers a compelling recipe for future edge robotics deployment.
sections.details:
FoldQuantVLA handles complex VLA architectures where language backbones and action experts interact by pre-folding basis transforms into weights. This suppresses activation outliers without runtime overhead and unlocks native low-bit integer inference.

It achieves clear speedups over floating-point engines on both desktop GPUs and Jetson AGX Orin. Furthermore, selective INT8 on specific language projections lifts physical robot success rates from 80.0% to 92.5%. This work provides practical and valuable guidelines for deploying foundation models on compute-constrained physical robots.

takeaways: Accelerating VLA models requires quantizing both weights and activations to low bits (W4A4) to leverage native hardware integer Tensor Cores.

For activation tensors shared across multiple consumer branches, a single basis transform must be maintained and its inverse pre-folded into weights (Consistent Folding) to prevent catastrophic coordinate mismatch errors.

Selective INT8—retaining only the language backbone output projections (o_proj and down_proj) at 8 bits—is a highly cost-effective design that prevents worst-case action failures and boosts real-robot success with only ~1 ms of added latency.
limitations: While effective on GR00T and $\pi_{0.5}$, substantial accuracy degradation was observed on architectures like SmolVLA and Evo-1, meaning universality across all VLA designs is not yet established.
Acceleration via true 4-bit Tensor Core math (native W4A4) depends on Orin and Ada-generation GPUs; some architectures like H100 fall back to INT8 internally.
Rank correlation between offline action cosine similarity and closed-loop task success is low, making it difficult to fully screen policy quality through numerical metrics alone.
